nodes.answer: The paper provides a comprehensive review of the literature on the evolution of understanding the economics of CDR, including theoretical and empirical cost estimates and projections for BECCS and DACCS.
nodes.paragraph: For instance, biomass-related CDR should consider temporal aspects of emissions, while DACCS faces uncertainties regarding the level and origin of energy consumption [ 22]. Lamb et al. (2024) identify a CDR gap , assessing poli - cies supporting CDR and finding that these are not sufficient to generate the CDR capacity to limit warming to 1.5 C [23]. The authors further discussed the competition between political interests aiming at expanding land-based removals and those that want to scale novel methods such as BECCS, DACCS, and biochar. In this paper, we examine the economic dimension of the CDR gap by providing a comprehensive review of the literature on how the understanding of the economics of CDR has evolved and what policy measures have been employed to address the challenge. First, we provide a review of theoretical and empirical cost estimates and pro - jections for BECCS and DACCS. We chose BECCS and DACCS because they are two technologies that are deemed to have reached relatively high technology readiness levels (TRL) (e.g., BECCS: 5 6, DACCS: 6 out of 10) with high inherent storage permanence [ 1].

nodes.label: Strategy
nodes.question: What is the significance of building a baseline for accounting the costs of subsidies and externalities?
nodes.answer: Building a baseline is important for understanding the complexity, size, design, and effects of subsidies and externalities, which could facilitate discussions for reform.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract Economic sectors that drive nature decline are heavily subsidized and produce large environmental externalities. Calls are increasing to reform or eliminatesubsidies and internalize the environmental costs of these sectors. We compile data on subsidies and externalities across six sectors driving biodiversity loss agriculture,fossil fuels, forestry, infrastructure, sheries and aquaculture, and mining. The most updated estimates suggest that subsidies to these sectors total between US$1.7and US$3.2 trillion annually, while environmental externalities range between US$10.5 and US$22.6 trillion annually. Moreover, data gaps suggest that these gures underestimate the global magnitude of subsidies and externalities. We discuss the need and opportunities of building a baseline to account for the costs of subsidies andexternalities of economic activities driving nature decline. A better understanding of the complexity, size, design, and effects of subsidies and externalities of such economicsectors could facilitate and expedite discussions to strengthen multilateral rules for their reform. Similarly, there is a lack of scholarly work on the capacity of ECAs as distinct financial institutions with unique organizational structures, competencies, resources, mandates, and institutional histories to effectively engage in clean energy finance. In this paper, we address these gaps in the literature. We first present descriptive statis - tics of ECA investments from 2005 2023 for select G20 countries. We show that despite some improvements in the post-Paris period, fossil fuel investments remain pervasive and growth in clean energy investments is minimal. For example, ECAs from China and Japan maintained in excess of $4 billion USD in average annual fossil fuel lending since 2015, while Canada and South Korea averaged over $2 billion USD in annual fossil fuel spending. However, there have also been notable increases in clean energy spending amongst some 1340 Climatic Change (2025) 178:40 ECAs, particularly the United Kingdom, which grew its annual clean energy lending from a pre-Paris average of $8.7 million USD to $64 million USD in the post-Paris period.

nodes.question: Which two procedures are mentioned for extracting factors from macroeconomic variables?
nodes.answer: The two procedures mentioned are the 2SKF method and Partial Least Squares (PLS).
nodes.paragraph: In this paper, we analyse the short-run relationship between economic activity and CO 2emissions in Spain, by tting a SADFM to annual rates of growth of Spanish CO 2 emissions with the factors extracted by 2SKF from a large set of Spanish macroeco-nomic variables. 2SKF is an unsupervised factor extraction procedure, which combinesinformation contained in all macroeconomic variables independently from the target variable. Additionally, we also consider factor extraction orientated towards pre- diction of the rate of growth of CO 2emissions. In particular, we extract factors using partial least squares (PLS) as proposed by Wold ( 1966 ). We conclude that the explana- tory power of selected economic variables is larger than that of common economic factors when the latter are extracted using the 2SKF procedure. However, the pre-dictive power of the common factors increases when they are extracted using PLS. We nd that the PLS common factors recover some explanatory power for explaining CO 2emissions beyond the information content of the selected individual economic indicators. Our results somehow differ from those found by Bennedsen et al. ( 2021 ) for the US economy as the outstanding predictors for CO 2emissions in Spain are private consumption and maritime transport of merchandise, while theirs rely more on IP .
